body.html:
Whole-corpus oracle · two rounds · final ruling

The whole-corpus oracle, tested twice: navigation beats packing for every retrieval shape

238 papers · 34 pages · 131k image tokens · Opus 4.8 both arms · oracle wins: 0 of 10 questions · the surviving shape is synthesis, not retrieval

Final ruling: NOT DEMONSTRATED — for retrieval
Holding all 238 published papers in one context (34 optical pages, 131k tokens vs ~849k as text) never beat a navigator agent with Grep over the same corpus: round 1 (lexically-anchored questions) navigator tied or won all five; round 2 (questions engineered so grep is structurally blind — semantic needles sharing zero content words with their targets, an absence proof, a multi-hop join) navigator 4/5 vs oracle 3/5. Two mechanisms explain it, both now measured.

Why the oracle loses retrieval

• The navigator is not grep — it is a model that spends semantics on generating lexical probes. One synonym hop (pointer→cursor, in-memory store→ETS) re-anchors an 'anchor-free' question. Only one question of ten truly resisted synonym-hopping — and there BOTH arms failed on corpus ambiguity, so the oracle bought no disambiguation.
• Whole-corpus reading pays a precision tax. The most diagnostic result: the oracle, with the target paper IN ITS WINDOW, attributed the answer to a sibling paper — right topic neighborhood, wrong document, full confidence. Dense optical context dilutes attribution exactly where retrieval needs it sharp.
• Keyword absence proofs are grep's home turf. A deterministic zero from one grep beats an oracle's 'I did not see it' across 34 pages.
• Oracle texture that has no scoreboard: negative knowledge (naming which papers do NOT contain a thing and why) and calibrated uncertainty (a ±2 band containing the truth while the navigator was confidently wrong). Real, but it never converted to a won question.

Scoreboard (both rounds)

RoundQuestion shapeOracleNavigator
1needle w/ lexical anchor (3 slugs)2/33/3
1contradiction synthesis (judged)✓ tie✓ tie
1cross-doc join (calibration score)✓ tie✓ tie
1aggregate count (key 14)12 ±2 honest18 confident-wrong
1corpus-scale ranking✗ salience-skewedexact counts
2semantic needle, no synonym route✗✗ (both failed — question ambiguity)
2semantic needle, synonym route exists✓ tie✓ tie
2semantic needle (pointer→cursor)✗ sibling misattribution✓ exact slug
2absence proof (keyword-shaped)✓ tie✓ tie
2multi-hop join✓ tie✓ tie

The rule this buys

If the answer lives in a few papers, grep. If the answer IS the corpus, pack.
Packing the knowledge base is worth its 131k tokens only when the task inherently reads most of the corpus anyway — whole-corpus synthesis briefs, cross-paper consistency sweeps, dedup audits, 'summarize everything about X'. There the honest text alternative is ~849k tokens, and 6.5× optical compression genuinely wins. That is the same law the duel series wrote: a delivery format for read-once prose synthesis — never a retrieval index, never a working substrate. Two standing caveats: verify any exact slug/ID from the pack with one grep before acting on it, and never pack what an agent will edit.

description: Two-round test of holding all 238 published papers in one context (34 optical pages, 131k image tokens vs ~849k as text) against a Grep-equipped navigator, both on Opus 4.8. The oracle won zero of ten questions: with lexical anchors the navigator ties or wins everything; with anchor-free semantic needles the navigator's synonym hop re-anchors the question while the oracle misattributes to sibling papers despite having the answer in-window. Final rule: if the answer lives in a few papers, grep; if the answer IS the corpus (whole-corpus synthesis, consistency sweeps, dedup audits), pack — that is the only shape where 6.5x optical compression of the knowledge base genuinely wins.
